points: Column with 12 sieve trays operated at 101 kilopascals and a reflux ratio of 3.0
Feed ethanol mole fraction 0.10; distillate ethanol mole fraction 0.82
Mean Murphree tray efficiency 64 % with a standard deviation of 5 %
Tray model prediction 58 % with a prediction uncertainty of 6 %
No weeping was detected and no entrainment was detected under the stated conditions
definitions: Murphree tray efficiency = the actual change in vapour composition across a tray divided by the change that equilibrium with the liquid leaving the tray would give
mole fraction = the amount of a component divided by the total amount of all components in the same mixture
standard deviation = the spread of the individual tray values about their mean
prediction uncertainty = the standard deviation of the model estimate under the stated input ranges
limits: Efficiency values apply to the ethanol and water system at the stated reflux ratio and pressure; foaming systems are outside the tested scope
figures: Fig. 1: Murphree tray efficiency by tray position, with the model prediction
prose: Tray efficiency was measured in a laboratory sieve-tray column charged with the ethanol and water system. The column held 12 sieve trays and ran at 101 kilopascals with a reflux ratio of 3.0. Vapour and liquid samples were drawn at each tray after the compositions had settled, and each sample was analysed in duplicate by the same operator on the same instrument. Feed ethanol mole fraction (the amount of ethanol divided by the total amount of all components in the mixture) was 0.10. The distillate ethanol mole fraction reached 0.82 at the stated reflux ratio. Murphree tray efficiency, the actual change in vapour composition across a tray divided by the change that equilibrium with the liquid leaving the tray would give, averaged 64 % across the column (standard deviation 5 %, the standard deviation being the spread of the individual tray values about their mean). Fig. 1 shows the efficiency by tray position. The tray model prediction was 58 %, and the prediction uncertainty, the standard deviation of the model estimate under the stated input ranges, was 6 %. The prediction sits below the measured mean at every tray position, and the gap between prediction and measurement is widest near the feed tray. The entrainment term of the model carries the gap, because the model holds entrainment at a fixed fraction of the vapour flow while the measured compositions track a falling entrainment rate up the column. No weeping was detected at the stated vapour rates, and no entrainment was detected by the tracer test at the column top. Hydraulic limits do not explain the gap. For the ethanol and water system at the stated reflux ratio and pressure, design calculations that use the measured mean efficiency rest on a firmer basis than calculations that use the model value, and foaming systems are outside the tested scope.

points: Packed bed of activated carbon, bed length 25 centimetres, bed void fraction 0.40, bed temperature 298 kelvin
Feed gas with a carbon dioxide fraction of 15 % in nitrogen
Breakthrough time 42 minutes at the stated feed conditions
Adsorption capacity 2.8 moles per kilogram of adsorbent, standard deviation 0.2, mean of 3 runs
Capacity retained 92 % after 6 regeneration cycles
definitions: breakthrough time = the time at which the outlet carbon dioxide fraction first rises above the detection threshold of the analyser
adsorption capacity = the amount of carbon dioxide held by the bed at saturation divided by the mass of adsorbent
standard deviation = the spread of the run values about their mean
bed void fraction = the fraction of the bed volume not occupied by solid
limits: Capacity values apply to dry feed gas; humid feed gas is outside the tested scope
figures: Fig. 1: outlet carbon dioxide fraction against time for the packed bed
prose: Breakthrough of carbon dioxide through a packed bed of activated carbon was measured at a bed temperature of 298 kelvin. The bed length was 25 centimetres, and the bed void fraction, the fraction of the bed volume not occupied by solid, was 0.40. Feed gas entered the bed with a carbon dioxide fraction of 15 % in nitrogen at a steady flow, and the outlet fraction was recorded by a single analyser from the start of each run. Fig. 1 shows the outlet fraction against time. Breakthrough time, the time at which the outlet carbon dioxide fraction first rises above the detection threshold of the analyser, was 42 minutes at the stated feed conditions. Adsorption capacity, the amount of carbon dioxide held by the bed at saturation divided by the mass of adsorbent, was 2.8 moles per kilogram of adsorbent (standard deviation 0.2 moles per kilogram, the standard deviation being the spread of the run values about their mean, over 3 runs). The capacity rests on the full area above the breakthrough curve, and the curve shape near breakthrough is steep, which keeps the unused fraction of the bed short. Regeneration under vacuum restored the bed between runs, and capacity retained after 6 regeneration cycles was 92 % of the first-cycle value. The retained capacity after cycling sits within the run-to-run spread of fresh beds, and no progressive loss was detected across the cycles under the stated regeneration conditions. The outlet record carries a flat opening stretch before the rise, and the flat stretch matches the passage of feed gas through the void space ahead of the adsorption front. Front movement through the bed is steady rather than dispersed, and the steep front keeps the mass transfer zone short relative to the bed length. For dry feed gas at the stated temperature and feed fraction, the bed holds the stated capacity at breakthrough, and humid feed gas is outside the tested scope.

points: Seeded cooling crystallization of an aqueous potassium nitrate solution; seed mass 2.5 grams per litre of solution
Cooling rate 0.3 kelvin per minute to a final temperature of 283 kelvin
Crystal yield 68 % of the salt dissolved at charge
Mean crystal size 240 micrometres with a standard deviation of 35 micrometres
Product purity 99.2 % by mass
Unseeded baseline yield 47 % under the same cooling programme
definitions: crystal yield = the mass of crystals recovered divided by the mass of salt dissolved at charge
mean crystal size = the arithmetic mean of the measured crystal diameters in the recovered product
standard deviation = the spread of the measured diameters about their mean
limits: Yield and size values apply to the stated cooling programme and seed loading; other salts are outside the tested scope
figures: Fig. 1: crystal size distribution for the seeded batch
prose: Seeded cooling crystallization of an aqueous potassium nitrate solution was run in a stirred batch crystallizer. Seed mass was 2.5 grams per litre of solution, added at the point of first saturation. The cooling rate was 0.3 kelvin per minute, held from the saturation point to a final temperature of 283 kelvin. Agitation held the crystals in suspension without visible breakage, and samples for size measurement were taken from the discharge slurry. Crystal yield, the mass of crystals recovered divided by the mass of salt dissolved at charge, was 68 %. The unseeded baseline yield under the same cooling programme was 47 %, and the baseline batches nucleated late in the cooling ramp with a wide spread of crystal sizes. Mean crystal size, the arithmetic mean of the measured crystal diameters in the recovered product, was 240 micrometres (standard deviation 35 micrometres, the standard deviation being the spread of the measured diameters about their mean). Fig. 1 shows the size distribution for the seeded batch. The distribution is single-peaked, and no secondary nucleation peak was detected in the fine end of the distribution under the stated agitation conditions. Product purity was 99.2 % by mass, with mother liquor inclusions carrying the impurity load. Seeding moves nucleation from a single uncontrolled event to the seed surface, and the yield gain over the baseline sits with the longer growth period that early seeding opens. Recovered crystals were washed with a small volume of chilled saturated solution and dried under vacuum before weighing, and the wash procedure was held identical across seeded and baseline batches. Size measurement used the same sieve stack and the same operator for every batch, and broken or twinned crystals were counted under a single stated rule. For the stated cooling programme and seed loading, the seeded batch gives the stated yield and size, and other salts are outside the tested scope.

points: Titanium dioxide catalyst loading 0.5 grams per litre
Initial dye concentration 20 milligrams per litre
Dye removal 87 % after 120 minutes of irradiation
Apparent rate constant 0.017 per minute from a first-order fit
Removal in the dark adsorption control 9 %; removal under irradiation with no catalyst 4 %
Activity retained 81 % after 5 reuse cycles
definitions: dye removal = the fall in dye concentration divided by the initial dye concentration
apparent rate constant = the rate constant obtained from a first-order fit to the concentration record, a model output rather than a measured quantity
limits: Removal values apply to the stated lamp spectrum and the stated dye; effluents with competing light absorbers are outside the tested scope
figures: Fig. 1: dye concentration against irradiation time, with the two control records
prose: Photocatalytic degradation of a dye solution was measured in a stirred reactor under a fixed lamp. Titanium dioxide catalyst loading was 0.5 grams per litre, and the initial dye concentration was 20 milligrams per litre. The suspension was stirred in the dark until adsorption settled before the lamp was switched on, and samples were filtered before analysis by the same procedure at every sampling point. Fig. 1 shows the concentration record. Dye removal, the fall in dye concentration divided by the initial dye concentration, reached 87 % after 120 minutes of irradiation. The apparent rate constant, the rate constant obtained from a first-order fit to the concentration record and a model output rather than a measured quantity, was 0.017 per minute. Removal in the dark adsorption control was 9 %, and removal under irradiation with no catalyst was 4 %. Adsorption and direct photolysis together account for a small share of the removal, and the gap between the controls and the full record sits with the irradiated catalyst. The first-order fit tracks the record closely over the opening stretch and drifts late in the run, where the falling concentration leaves fewer dye molecules near the catalyst surface. Activity retained after 5 reuse cycles was 81 % of the first-cycle removal, with the catalyst recovered by filtration and washed between cycles. No abrupt activity loss was detected between cycles under the stated recovery procedure. Lamp output was checked against a reference cell before each run, and the reactor geometry, stirring rate, and sampling positions were held fixed across the catalyst record and the two controls. Sample handling in the dark after withdrawal kept post-sampling reaction out of the record, and every concentration point rests on the same calibration line. For the stated lamp spectrum and the stated dye, the catalyst holds the stated removal and rate, and effluents with competing light absorbers are outside the tested scope.

points: Goal: tune a proportional-integral-derivative loop for a temperature process and obtain a stated response to a set point step
Process model: first-order lag with a time constant of 4.5 minutes, a dead time of 1.2 minutes, and a process gain of 1.8
Tuned settings: controller gain 3.4, integral time 2.4 minutes, derivative time 0.60 minutes
Set point step 10 % of span
Closed-loop result: overshoot 12 % of the step and a settling time of 9 minutes, with no steady-state offset detected
definitions: PID = proportional-integral-derivative, a controller that acts on the error, the accumulated error, and the rate of change of the error
time constant = the time a first-order process needs to complete the characteristic share of its total change after a step input
dead time = the delay between a change in the input and the first movement of the output
process gain = the change in output divided by the change in input, each at steady state
settling time = the time after a step at which the output enters the stated tolerance band about the set point and stays inside the band
overshoot = the peak excursion of the output beyond the set point, divided by the step size
limits: The settings apply to the stated process model; a process with a longer dead time relative to its lag is outside the worked scope
prose: This tutorial tunes a PID (proportional-integral-derivative) loop, a controller that acts on the error, the accumulated error, and the rate of change of the error. You start from a process model, apply a stated tuning rule, and finish with settings you can check against a recorded step response. The outcome to expect is a response that overshoots modestly and settles without offset. Audience: you need a first-order process model and a way to record the loop response. The process model for the worked example is a first-order lag with a time constant of 4.5 minutes, the time constant being the time a first-order process needs to complete the characteristic share of its total change after a step input. Dead time, the delay between a change in the input and the first movement of the output, is 1.2 minutes. Process gain, the change in output divided by the change in input with each at steady state, is 1.8. Enter the three model values into the tuning rule for a lag with a short dead time. The rule returns a controller gain of 3.4, an integral time of 2.4 minutes, and a derivative time of 0.60 minutes. Warning: load the integral term only after the loop is closed and tracking, because an integral term that accumulates during a long manual period drives the output hard at the switch. Apply a set point step of 10 % of span and record the response. Overshoot, the peak excursion of the output beyond the set point divided by the step size, is 12 % of the step. Settling time, the time after a step at which the output enters the stated tolerance band about the set point and stays inside the band, is 9 minutes. No steady-state offset was detected in the recorded response under the stated settings. Check the result by comparing the recorded overshoot and settling time with the values the tuning rule predicts for the model; a response far outside the prediction points to a wrong model value, most often the dead time. The settings apply to the stated process model; a process with a longer dead time relative to its lag is outside the worked scope.

points: Goal: compute the available net positive suction head for a pump drawing water from an open tank and compare the value with the pump requirement
Atmospheric pressure head 10.3 metres of water
Vapour pressure head 0.43 metres; static suction lift 2.0 metres; suction line friction loss 1.1 metres
Available head 6.8 metres from the stated terms
Required head from the pump curve 4.5 metres; margin 2.3 metres
definitions: NPSH = net positive suction head, the total head at the pump inlet measured above the vapour pressure head of the liquid
available head = the NPSH the suction layout delivers at the stated flow
required head = the NPSH the pump needs at the stated flow, read from the pump curve
static suction lift = the vertical distance from the liquid surface in the tank to the pump centreline
limits: The calculation holds for the stated liquid temperature and suction layout; a hotter liquid or a longer suction line is outside the worked scope
prose: This worked example computes the available NPSH (net positive suction head, the total head at the pump inlet measured above the vapour pressure head of the liquid) for a pump drawing water from an open tank. You finish with a margin you can compare directly with the pump requirement. Audience: you need the suction layout, the liquid temperature, and the pump curve. Inputs first. Atmospheric pressure head at the tank surface is 10.3 metres of water. Vapour pressure head at the stated temperature is 0.43 metres. Static suction lift, the vertical distance from the liquid surface in the tank to the pump centreline, is 2.0 metres. Suction line friction loss at the stated flow is 1.1 metres. Subtract the vapour pressure head, the lift, and the friction loss from the atmospheric head. The available head, the NPSH the suction layout delivers at the stated flow, is 6.8 metres. Required head, the NPSH the pump needs at the stated flow and read from the pump curve, is 4.5 metres. The margin of available head over required head is 2.3 metres. What the result shows: the layout delivers more head than the pump needs at the stated flow, and the margin absorbs small errors in the friction estimate. Check the arithmetic by adding the loss terms back to the available head; the sum returns the atmospheric head. Warning: the margin shrinks fast as the liquid warms, because vapour pressure head climbs with temperature while the other terms barely move. Recheck the vapour pressure head at the highest temperature the tank reaches before accepting the layout. A layout that fails the comparison cavitates at the impeller inlet, and cavitation shows first as noise, vibration, and a falling discharge head before any visible damage appears. Tank level matters in the same direction: a falling level raises the lift term and eats the margin from the other side, and a low-level alarm set with the margin in mind guards both failure paths. The calculation holds for the stated liquid temperature and suction layout; a hotter liquid or a longer suction line is outside the worked scope.

points: Goal: size a shell-and-tube exchanger for a stated duty and check the selected area against a fouling allowance
Duty 850 kilowatts; the hot stream enters at 363 kelvin and leaves at 323 kelvin
The cold stream enters at 293 kelvin and leaves at 313 kelvin
End temperature differences 50 kelvin and 30 kelvin; log mean temperature difference 39.1 kelvin
Overall heat transfer coefficient 0.620 kilowatts per square metre per kelvin
Clean area 35 square metres; fouling correction factor 0.92; selected area 38 square metres
definitions: LMTD = log mean temperature difference, the driving force for heat transfer averaged over the exchanger length for the stated terminal temperatures
overall heat transfer coefficient = the heat flow per unit area per unit temperature difference across the tube wall and the films on both sides
fouling correction factor = the fraction of the clean coefficient expected to remain in service after fouling deposits form
limits: The sizing holds for the stated terminal temperatures and a single-pass arrangement; a changed temperature programme is outside the worked scope
prose: This tutorial sizes a shell-and-tube exchanger from a stated duty and four terminal temperatures. You finish with a selected area and a fouling check. Audience: you need stream temperatures, a duty, and a coefficient estimate for the fluids in question. Inputs first. Duty is 850 kilowatts. The hot stream enters at 363 kelvin and leaves at 323 kelvin. The cold stream enters at 293 kelvin and leaves at 313 kelvin. Compute the driving force at each end of the exchanger. The end temperature differences are 50 kelvin at the hot inlet end and 30 kelvin at the hot outlet end. The LMTD (log mean temperature difference, the driving force for heat transfer averaged over the exchanger length for the stated terminal temperatures) is 39.1 kelvin. The overall heat transfer coefficient, the heat flow per unit area per unit temperature difference across the tube wall and the films on both sides, is 0.620 kilowatts per square metre per kelvin. Divide the duty by the product of the coefficient and the LMTD. Clean area is 35 square metres. Apply the fouling allowance before selecting a shell. The fouling correction factor, the fraction of the clean coefficient expected to remain in service after fouling deposits form, is 0.92. Selected area is 38 square metres. Tube count and shell diameter follow from the selected area under the stated tube geometry and pass arrangement. What the result shows: the selected area carries the duty at the fouled coefficient, with the allowance held in area rather than in a higher clean coefficient. Check the sizing by multiplying the fouled coefficient, the selected area, and the LMTD; the product returns the duty within rounding. Warning: a temperature cross, where the cold outlet passes the hot outlet, breaks the LMTD calculation for a single-pass shell, and a crossed programme needs a multi-pass arrangement or a different configuration. The sizing holds for the stated terminal temperatures and a single-pass arrangement; a changed temperature programme is outside the worked scope.

points: Setting: biodiesel production from waste cooking oil with an immobilised lipase catalyst
Enzyme loading 6 % by mass of oil; methanol to oil molar ratio 4.5
Reaction time 24 hours at 313 kelvin
Oil conversion 94 %
Conversion after 8 reuse cycles 88 %
definitions: lipase = an enzyme that catalyses the reaction of oils with methanol to form biodiesel
immobilised = fixed on a solid support for recovery and reuse
oil conversion = the fraction of the charged oil converted to biodiesel
methanol to oil molar ratio = the amount of methanol divided by the amount of oil, each in moles
prose: Waste cooking oil carries a disposal cost and a variable composition, and a production route that tolerates the variability has direct value for small biodiesel plants. This study tests an immobilised lipase route, lipase being an enzyme that catalyses the reaction of oils with methanol to form biodiesel, and immobilised meaning fixed on a solid support for recovery and reuse. Enzyme loading was 6 % by mass of oil, and the methanol to oil molar ratio, the amount of methanol divided by the amount of oil with each in moles, was 4.5. Batches ran for 24 hours at 313 kelvin with stepwise methanol addition. Oil conversion, the fraction of the charged oil converted to biodiesel, reached 94 %. Conversion after 8 reuse cycles of the same catalyst charge was 88 %. Glycerol separated cleanly from the product under the stated settling procedure, and no soap formation was detected in the product at the stated feed water content. The immobilised catalyst holds conversion across reuse cycles with a shallow decline, and stepwise methanol addition carries the tolerance to the variable feed. The route suits small plants that value catalyst reuse over batch speed.

points: Setting: lithium recovery from a salt lake brine with a selective sorbent
Feed lithium concentration 240 milligrams per litre; magnesium to lithium ratio in the feed 18
Sorbent capacity 14 milligrams of lithium per gram of sorbent
Extraction efficiency 91 % of the lithium in the feed
Product magnesium to lithium ratio 1.6
Capacity loss 3 % over 30 loading cycles
definitions: sorbent = a solid that takes up a target ion from solution on its surface and releases the ion into a second solution
extraction efficiency = the amount of lithium recovered in the product stream divided by the amount of lithium in the feed
magnesium to lithium ratio = the mass of magnesium divided by the mass of lithium in the same stream
prose: Salt lake brines hold lithium at low concentration beside a large excess of magnesium, and a separation that rejects magnesium decides the cost of lithium recovery from the resource. This study measures a selective sorbent route, a sorbent being a solid that takes up a target ion from solution on its surface and releases the ion into a second solution. Feed lithium concentration was 240 milligrams per litre, and the magnesium to lithium ratio in the feed, the mass of magnesium divided by the mass of lithium in the same stream, was 18. Packed columns of the sorbent were loaded with brine, washed, and stripped in a repeating cycle. Sorbent capacity reached 14 milligrams of lithium per gram of sorbent. Extraction efficiency, the amount of lithium recovered in the product stream divided by the amount of lithium in the feed, was 91 %. The product magnesium to lithium ratio was 1.6. Capacity loss over 30 loading cycles was 3 %. The sorbent separates lithium from magnesium by a wide margin in a single loading stage, and the shallow capacity loss across cycles keeps the separation open to continuous operation. Brine treatment with a selective sorbent is a workable front end for lithium recovery at the stated feed composition.

points: A single microchannel of width 600 micrometres delivers 0.8 kilograms of product per day
Target plant throughput 400 kilograms per day
A numbering-up array of 500 channels reaches the target throughput at the stated per-channel rate
Pressure drop per channel 85 kilopascals at the stated flow
Residence time 45 seconds in a single channel
Flow distribution across a large parallel array is unmeasured, and maldistribution across channels is the open question
definitions: microchannel = a channel with a width below one millimetre, where surface forces and short diffusion paths govern the flow
numbering-up = replication of identical channels in parallel to raise throughput, in place of enlargement of a single channel
residence time = the average time a fluid element spends inside the channel
limits: The study covers numbering-up of identical channels; enlargement of a single channel is outside the study scope
prose: Microchannel reactors carry fast and exothermic reactions with a control that stirred vessels cannot match, and a microchannel, a channel with a width below one millimetre where surface forces and short diffusion paths govern the flow, gives that control at laboratory scale. A single channel of width 600 micrometres delivers 0.8 kilograms of product per day. Plant demand sits far above the single-channel rate, and the target plant throughput in this study is 400 kilograms per day. Numbering-up, the replication of identical channels in parallel to raise throughput in place of enlargement of a single channel, is the established route from the laboratory device to plant rates. An array of 500 channels reaches the target throughput at the stated per-channel rate. Established work covers reaction performance inside a single channel and inside small arrays. Flow distribution across a large parallel array is unmeasured, and maldistribution across channels is the open question: a channel starved of flow runs long, a channel flooded with flow runs short, and the product record of the array carries both faults. Pressure drop per channel is 85 kilopascals at the stated flow, and residence time, the average time a fluid element spends inside the channel, is 45 seconds. This study measures flow distribution across a full array with tracer injection at the shared inlet and sampling at grouped outlets, and the study covers numbering-up of identical channels; enlargement of a single channel is outside the study scope.

points: Solvent loss by degradation 0.42 kilograms per tonne of carbon dioxide captured
Heat-stable salt content 3.1 % of the solvent inventory at the end of the campaign
Pilot campaign length 2000 hours on a coal flue gas slipstream
Oxygen partial pressure in the treated gas 21 kilopascals
Degradation rates to be measured at 313 kelvin, 333 kelvin, and 353 kelvin
The split of solvent degradation between the oxidative route and the thermal route in operating solvent is unmeasured
definitions: heat-stable salts = degradation products that bind the amine solvent and are not released in the regenerator
degradation rate = the loss of active amine per unit time under stated conditions
flue gas slipstream = a side draw from the main flue gas flow, treated in the pilot unit
limits: The study covers one amine solvent on a coal flue gas slipstream; natural gas flue gas is outside the study scope
prose: Amine solvents capture carbon dioxide from flue gas in the absorber and release the gas in the regenerator, and the same solvent charge circulates between the two vessels for the life of a campaign. Solvent loss by degradation runs at 0.42 kilograms per tonne of carbon dioxide captured in the pilot record, and degradation, not leakage or carry-over, carries most of the solvent cost of the process. Heat-stable salts, degradation products that bind the amine solvent and are not released in the regenerator, reached 3.1 % of the solvent inventory at the end of the campaign. The campaign ran for 2000 hours on a coal flue gas slipstream, a side draw from the main flue gas flow treated in the pilot unit. Oxygen partial pressure in the treated gas was 21 kilopascals. Established work reports degradation rates for fresh solvent in bench apparatus under a single route at a time, oxidative or thermal. The split of solvent degradation between the oxidative route and the thermal route in operating solvent is unmeasured, and the split decides whether reclaiming, oxygen exclusion, or temperature control carries the remedy. This study measures the degradation rate, the loss of active amine per unit time under stated conditions, at 313 kelvin, 333 kelvin, and 353 kelvin in solvent drawn from the pilot loop, with the oxidative route isolated by oxygen-free duplicates. The study covers one amine solvent on a coal flue gas slipstream; natural gas flue gas is outside the study scope.

points: Rotational rheometer with a concentric cylinder geometry and a measuring gap of 1.0 millimetres
Sample volume 19 millilitres per measurement
Measurement temperature 323 kelvin, held by a circulating bath
Pre-shear period 60 seconds and rest period 300 seconds before each measurement
Shear rate sweep from 0.1 to 1000 reciprocal seconds
Replicates 4 per sample; repeatability 2.4 % as a coefficient of variation
definitions: rheometry = the measurement of the flow properties of a fluid under controlled shear
shear rate = the velocity gradient imposed on the sample across the measuring gap
coefficient of variation = the standard deviation of repeated measurements divided by their mean, a measure of spread
yield stress = the stress below which the sample does not flow
limits: The procedure covers the stated temperature and shear rate range; samples with settled solids are outside the procedure scope
prose: Rheometry, the measurement of the flow properties of a fluid under controlled shear, followed a fixed procedure for every drilling fluid sample. A rotational rheometer with a concentric cylinder geometry and a measuring gap of 1.0 millimetres held the sample. Sample volume was 19 millilitres per measurement, loaded with a syringe to keep air out of the gap. Measurement temperature was 323 kelvin, held by a circulating bath, and the sample rested in the geometry until the temperature reading settled before any shear was applied. Warning: an exposed sample edge dries during long runs and stiffens the record, and a solvent trap covered the sample for every measurement in the sweep. Each measurement opened with a pre-shear period of 60 seconds at the top rate, and a rest period of 300 seconds followed before the sweep began. The shear rate sweep, the velocity gradient imposed on the sample across the measuring gap, ran from 0.1 to 1000 reciprocal seconds in ascending steps, with the matching descending sweep recorded straight after. Replicates numbered 4 per sample, each from a fresh loading. Repeatability was 2.4 % as a coefficient of variation, the coefficient of variation being the standard deviation of repeated measurements divided by their mean, a measure of spread. A reference oil of certified viscosity verified the instrument at the start of each session, and a session opened only after the reference reading fell inside its certified band. Yield stress, the stress below which the sample does not flow, and the flow curve came from a Herschel and Bulkley fit to the descending sweep. The procedure covers the stated temperature and shear rate range; samples with settled solids are outside the procedure scope.

points: Calibration with 6 levels spanning 0.05 to 25 milligrams per litre
Internal standard held at 5 milligrams per litre in every vial
Coefficient of determination 0.998 for the calibration line
Limit of quantification 0.08 milligrams per litre
Replicate injections 3 per level; relative standard deviation 1.7 %
Column length 30 metres; split ratio 20
definitions: internal standard = a compound added at a fixed concentration to every vial, against which the analyte response is ratioed
coefficient of determination = the fraction of the variance in the response that the calibration line accounts for, a fit statistic rather than a measured quantity
limit of quantification = the lowest concentration at which the method reports a value with the stated precision
relative standard deviation = the standard deviation of repeated measurements divided by their mean, expressed as a percentage and a measure of spread
limits: The calibration covers the stated range and the stated sample matrix; samples above the top level are diluted into the range before analysis
prose: Calibration for the gas chromatography method used standards prepared in the sample matrix and carried through the full analysis procedure. Calibration used 6 levels spanning 0.05 to 25 milligrams per litre, prepared by serial dilution from a single stock on the day of analysis. An internal standard, a compound added at a fixed concentration to every vial against which the analyte response is ratioed, was held at 5 milligrams per litre in every vial. Warning: the internal standard goes into the vial before any dilution step, because a standard added after dilution cannot correct losses in the dilution itself. The column length was 30 metres, and injections ran at a split ratio of 20 under a fixed temperature programme for standards and samples alike. Replicate injections numbered 3 per level. The coefficient of determination, the fraction of the variance in the response that the calibration line accounts for and a fit statistic rather than a measured quantity, was 0.998. Relative standard deviation, the standard deviation of repeated measurements divided by their mean, expressed as a percentage and a measure of spread, was 1.7 % across the levels. The limit of quantification, the lowest concentration at which the method reports a value with the stated precision, was 0.08 milligrams per litre. A certified reference material, analysed as an unknown in each batch, verified the calibration by an independent route, and a batch was accepted only where the reference value fell inside its certified interval. Standard preparation used the same glassware class and the same balance for every level, and prepared standards stood capped until injection to keep evaporation out of the record. The calibration covers the stated range and the stated sample matrix; samples above the top level are diluted into the range before analysis.

points: Pilot fluidised bed combustor rated at 150 kilowatts thermal
Operating record 640 hours on the stated coal
Bed temperature 1123 kelvin held across the record
Combustion efficiency 98.6 %
Sulphur capture 89 % at a calcium to sulphur molar ratio of 2.1
Sorbent utilisation 42 %
Nitrogen oxide emissions 180 milligrams per cubic metre of dry flue gas
definitions: fluidised bed = a bed of solid particles suspended in a rising gas stream, mixing as a fluid
combustion efficiency = the fraction of the fuel carbon that leaves the combustor as carbon dioxide
sulphur capture = the fraction of the fuel sulphur retained in the bed solids
sorbent utilisation = the fraction of the charged calcium that has reacted with sulphur
limits: One coal type was tested; high-ash coals are outside the tested scope
The unit is pilot scale; heat transfer surfaces of a full-scale unit are outside the tested scope
prose: The pilot campaign supports one claim at the tested scope: a fluidised bed, a bed of solid particles suspended in a rising gas stream and mixing as a fluid, burns the stated coal cleanly at pilot scale with in-bed sulphur capture. The combustor is rated at 150 kilowatts thermal, and the operating record covers 640 hours on the stated coal. Bed temperature held at 1123 kelvin across the record. Combustion efficiency, the fraction of the fuel carbon that leaves the combustor as carbon dioxide, was 98.6 %. Sulphur capture, the fraction of the fuel sulphur retained in the bed solids, was 89 % at a calcium to sulphur molar ratio of 2.1. Sorbent utilisation, the fraction of the charged calcium that has reacted with sulphur, was 42 %. Nitrogen oxide emissions were 180 milligrams per cubic metre of dry flue gas. The claim rests on the combination of the three records: efficiency and sulphur capture held together across the full campaign, and emissions stayed within the band the bed temperature sets. Bed inventory held steady across the campaign with ash withdrawal matched to the feed ash, and the gas record rests on continuous analysers checked daily against certified span gases, with the solids record resting on bed samples drawn at each withdrawal. Two limits bound the claim. One coal type was tested, and high-ash coals are outside the tested scope. The unit is pilot scale, and heat transfer surfaces of a full-scale unit are outside the tested scope.

points: Molar flux of a species through a stagnant film, stated by the Fick relation
Diffusion coefficient taken at a film temperature of 298 kelvin for the stated species and medium pair
A boundary case stands at thin films, where the concentration profile stays close to linear
definitions: J = molar flux of the species, the amount of the species crossing a unit area per unit time
D = diffusion coefficient of the species in the film medium
c = concentration of the species in the film
x = distance across the film, measured from the interface
limits: The relation in the stated form holds for a dilute species in a stagnant film, and the linear profile holds for films thinner than 1 millimetre
prose: Gas absorption into a liquid film, and drying of a wet solid, both rest on transport through a thin stagnant layer at the interface. The molar flux J, the amount of a species crossing a unit area per unit time, states the transport rate through the film. The Fick relation gives the flux as the negative product of the diffusion coefficient and the concentration gradient across the film: J equals minus D multiplied by the change in c over the change in x, where D is the diffusion coefficient of the species in the film medium, c is the concentration of the species in the film, and x is the distance across the film, measured from the interface. The negative sign carries the direction of transport: the flux runs from high concentration toward low concentration, against the direction in which c rises. The diffusion coefficient in the relation is the value at a film temperature of 298 kelvin for the stated species and medium pair, and the coefficient belongs to the pair rather than to the species alone. A boundary case stands next to the relation. For films thinner than 1 millimetre, the concentration profile stays close to linear, and the gradient in the relation can be read as the concentration difference across the film divided by the film thickness. At a uniform concentration the gradient vanishes, and the flux vanishes with the gradient. The relation in the stated form holds for a dilute species in a stagnant film; a concentrated mixture carries a bulk flow term that the stated form omits.
